blocks.text: Madchester, also known as Baggy or the Second Summer of Love, denotes a broad musical and cultural phenomenon originating in Manchester, England in 1987. The scene emerged as a manifestation of an emerging music driven youth culture within the city, gaining prominence from the late-1980s and peaking into the early-1990s. Madchester has a wide range of associations, including 1960s pop culture and psychedelia, baggy and casual fashion (typified by the bucket hat), a vast range of musical genres such as indie rock, post-punk, acid house, dance and electronica, as well as a vibrant hedonistic nightlife which emerged as part of the developing rave scene. The movement achieved widespread recognition through the British music press in 1989-90 after various Mancunian musical acts achieved mainstream success.

Key musical groups associated with the Madchester scene include the Stone Roses, Happy Mondays, Inspiral Carpets, The Charlatans, James, and 808 State. The prevalence of drug use (notably MDMA), and the seminal Haçienda nightclub significantly shaped the scene. The Haçienda was opened in 1982, owned by Factory Records and New Order; it became the focal point of the Mancunian music scene during its tenure, with Madchester acts, as well as pre-Madchester bands (such as the Smiths) performing there on various occasions. The club's manager, Tony Wilson, coined the term 'Madchester'. The Stone Roses' Spike Island gig in May 1990 was also regarded as a key moment for Madchester, referred to as "Woodstock for the E generation". This was followed by a period of domination by Manchester acts in the British music charts during the summer, making 1990 the peak of Madchester.

The movement's momentum slowly dissipated following the inactivity of central groups such as the Stone Roses and Happy Mondays. James, the Inspiral Carpets, the Charlatans, and 808 State continued to record with varying degrees of success throughout the 1990s, but they were no longer seen as part of a localized Manchester movement. Happy Mondays and the Stone Roses released follow-up albums in 1992 and 1994 respectively, but both were troubled and didn't live up to expectations. The Haçienda also experienced decline and financial strain, closing in temporarily in 1991 and permanently 1997. Going into the mid-1990s, bands who were influenced by the Madchester scene with similar indie-rock roots came to be regarded as Britpop and other guitar-driven genres as the zeitgeist shifted. More dance-orientated parts of the movement became absorbed by the broader rave and techno scenes, as well as the more working class 'Casuals' who continued with football hooliganism and 'Lad Culture'.
Early Manchester scene and the Haçienda

The origins of Madchester can be traced to the early 1980s Manchester music scene, which was shaped by post-punk and alternative acts such as Joy Division/New Order and The Smiths. The opening of The Haçienda nightclub in May 1982 by Factory Records, New Order and Tony Wilson became a key development in Manchester's underground culture. Initially hosting alternative bands alongside international acts, the club gradually became a central meeting point for the city's music scene.

In 1986, The Haçienda became one of the first British clubs to regularly play house music, helping introduce acid house to British audiences and contributing to the Second Summer of Love. By 1987, the club had grown significantly in popularity, hosting performances from influential American house artists such as Frankie Knuckles and Adonis.

Warehouse parties and informal raves also played an important role in the development of Madchester. These events combined live guitar music with emerging electronic sounds, reflecting the DIY and working-class identity associated with the movement. The Stone Roses' early warehouse performances, including the "Warehouse 1, The Flower Show" event in 1985, helped establish their following, while DJs such as Dave Booth helped connect Manchester's indie and dance music scenes.
Initial Chart Successes and Media Recognition (1987–1989)

Madchester artists began achieving wider recognition in the late 1980s through the independent music scene. Happy Mondays' debut album reached number four on the UK Independent Albums Chart, while The Stone Roses' "Sally Cinnamon" became an influential indie hit in 1987.

In 1988, The Stone Roses released "Elephant Stone", while Happy Mondays released "Wrote for Luck" and Bummed. Around the same time, A Guy Called Gerald released "Voodoo Ray", an influential acid house track that highlighted the growing relationship between Manchester's indie and dance scenes.

By 1989, the British music press had begun identifying Manchester as the centre of a developing cultural movement. The Stone Roses' self-titled debut album, released in May 1989, received widespread critical acclaim and became one of the most influential British debut albums, helping establish Madchester as a major force in alternative music.

Madchester reached its peak between 1989 and 1990, becoming one of the defining movements in British popular culture. The Stone Roses achieved major success with "Fools Gold", while Happy Mondays reached their commercial peak with Pills 'n' Thrills and Bellyaches in 1990. Other acts associated with the movement, including 808 State, The Charlatans and Inspiral Carpets, also achieved mainstream success.

The Haçienda became the centre of Manchester's nightlife, blending indie rock, acid house and electronic music. The Stone Roses' Spike Island concert on 27 May 1990, attended by approximately 27,000 people, became one of the most iconic events associated with the movement.

Madchester also influenced fashion and youth culture, with baggy clothing, sportswear and psychedelic imagery becoming closely associated with the scene. Its combination of guitar music and dance culture distinguished it from previous British alternative movements.

Madchester began to decline in the early 1990s due to internal difficulties, changing musical trends and problems affecting key figures and venues. The Stone Roses became inactive following a legal dispute with Silvertone Records, preventing them from releasing new material during the height of their popularity. Happy Mondays struggled with financial and personal difficulties during the production of their follow-up album Yes Please!, while other groups associated with the scene increasingly pursued separate musical directions. The Haçienda also faced growing financial and social pressures due to increased security costs, declining alcohol sales and police scrutiny surrounding drug use. Although the club temporarily closed in 1991 and later reopened, it never regained the influence it had during the movement's peak.

By 1992, the term "Madchester" had largely fallen out of mainstream use as attention shifted towards grunge, electronic music developments and the emerging Britpop movement. Despite its short lifespan, Madchester had a lasting influence on British music, particularly through its fusion of indie rock, psychedelia and dance culture.

Madchester's influence continued throughout the 1990s and beyond, particularly through Britpop and later alternative music. Bands such as Oasis drew inspiration from The Stone Roses' sound and image, while the movement helped establish Manchester as one of Britain's most important musical cities. The Haçienda's legacy, alongside the music of The Stone Roses, Happy Mondays and other associated acts, has contributed to Madchester's reputation as one of the most significant British music movements of the late 20th century.

At its peak, Madchester fashion combined elements of Northern working-class street style, football casual culture, psychedelia and the emerging rave scene. The style was characterised by loose-fitting clothing, reflecting both the influence of 1960s and 1970s counterculture and the practical needs of a dance-oriented youth culture.

Baggy clothing was central to the aesthetic, with oversized T-shirts, loose jumpers, wide-legged jeans, flared trousers, sportswear and bucket hats becoming closely associated with the movement. The emphasis on comfort and movement reflected the connection between Madchester's guitar music and club culture, particularly the influence of The Haçienda and acid house. The style was often relatively unisex, with men and women adopting similar silhouettes and clothing choices.

Psychedelic influences were visible through colourful patterns, retro designs and references to the 1960s Summer of Love, while football casual influences contributed brands such as Adidas and Reebok trainers, outdoor jackets and other sportswear. Vintage clothing, particularly wide flares and second-hand garments, was also popular, creating a distinctive blend of retro and contemporary styles.

Graphic T-shirts, often featuring Manchester-related slogans or psychedelic artwork, became a notable part of the look. Hairstyles such as Shaun Ryder's centre-parted "curtains" and Ian Brown's longer, mod-influenced style also became associated with the movement.

Although the style varied between individuals and regions, the overall Madchester aesthetic was defined by baggy silhouettes, casual sportswear, psychedelic imagery and a confident Northern identity. Its influence continued into the 1990s, particularly through Britpop, where elements of the look were adopted by bands such as Oasis.
